title: Understanding the Law of Large Numbers
text:
Let’s imagine a scenario in which a person flips a fair coin ten times, and, by chance, it lands heads eight times. Since the probability of a fair coin landing heads is 50%, an 80% heads rate seems somewhat illogical. This raises a classic question: If we continue flipping the coin, should we expect a string of tails to “make up” for these extra heads?
This question both illustrates the intuition behind the Law of Large Numbers and reveals one of the most common misunderstandings about it.
The law of large numbers states that, under appropriate conditions, as the number of observations increases, the average of the results from multiple observations will approach the expected value. For a fair coin, the expected proportion of heads is 0.5. However, if the coin is flipped only a few times, the observed proportion may deviate significantly from 0.5. As the number of flips increases, this proportion typically becomes more stable.
Mathematically, if we observe values (X_1, X_2…X_n), their sample average is
\[
\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.
\]
The Law of Large Numbers tells that, as (n) becomes larger and larger,
\[
\bar{X}_n \rightarrow E[X],
\]
where (E[X]) is the expected value of the underlying random variable.
For a coin flip, we can define heads as 1 and tails as 0. For a fair coin,
\[
E[X] = 0.5.
\]
So if we flip the coin again and again, the average of these zeros and ones tends to move toward 0.5.

title: Understanding the Law of Large Numbers
text:
Why Is This Unintuitive?
Surprisingly, the law of large numbers does not imply that random outcomes will actively correct themselves.
Suppose that eight out of the first ten coin flips result in heads. Most people’s common reaction might be to think that the probability of getting tails must now be higher so that the overall ratio can return to 50%. This is actually a classic example of a fallacy.
If the coin tosses are independent of one another, then the probability of getting heads on the eleventh toss is still exactly 50%. The coin does not “remember” what happened before.
So, how does the average eventually converge toward 50%?
The answer is not “correction,” but dilution.
After ten tosses, the first ten observations make up the entire sample. After 1,000 tosses, these first ten observations account for only 1% of the sample; after 10,000 tosses, they account for only 0.1%. The initial anomaly hasn’t disappeared, but its impact on the overall average becomes increasingly small.
In other words, the law of large numbers holds true because, as the number of observations increases, the influence of early random fluctuations becomes increasingly negligible.

title: Understanding the Law of Large Numbers
section: More Data Does Not Mean Perfect Data
text:
More Data Does Not Mean Perfect Data
Another common misconception is that a large sample size will always yield results that perfectly match the expected value. However, the law does not guarantee this.
Even if you flip a coin thousands of times, the proportion of heads might be 49.7% or 50.4%, rather than exactly 50%. Random fluctuations still occur. The key point is that as the sample size increases, the frequency of large deviations decreases.
The importance of this concept extends far beyond coin flipping. Economists use sample means to estimate wages, unemployment rates, consumer spending, and many other indicators. A survey of 20 people may be strongly influenced by a few outliers. Larger, representative samples are typically more stable because individual random variations have less impact on the population mean.
This is also why collecting more data improves statistical estimates. More observations do not eliminate randomness, but they reduce the impact of random fluctuations in any small portion of the sample.

title: My First Blog Post
text:
The Law of Large Numbers does not say that luck “balances itself out” because future outcomes compensate for past ones. Instead, it says that as more independent observations accumulate, unusual early outcomes become a smaller part of the overall average.
A useful way to remember the idea is:
Large numbers do not correct randomness—they dilute it.
That distinction is what makes the Law of Large Numbers both powerful and easy to misunderstand.

A practical way to remember this concept is:
Large numbers do not correct for randomness—they merely dilute it.
It is precisely this distinction that makes the Law of Large Numbers both powerful and prone to misunderstanding.

title: Who Had the Biggest Impact in the 2025–26 NBA Season?
text:
Basketball fans often judge players first and foremost by one statistic: points per game. While scoring is certainly important, it doesn’t fully reflect a player’s contribution. Players can add value through passing, rebounding, efficient shooting, defense, and simply helping their team perform better on the court.
This has sparked my interest in a broader question: Which players had the greatest overall impact during the 2025–26 NBA regular season?

title: Who Had the Biggest Impact in the 2025–26 NBA Season?
text:
Collecting the Data
I collected player statistics from Basketball-Reference using the rvest package in R. I scraped two publicly available tables: one containing traditional per-game statistics and another containing advanced statistics.
The traditional data included points, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks per game. The advanced dataset included measures such as True Shooting Percentage (TS%), Box Plus/Minus (BPM), Win Shares, and Value Over Replacement Player (VORP).
To keep the scraping process lightweight, I only requested the two pages needed for the analysis and inserted a short delay between requests. The raw tables were saved before any cleaning so that the analysis could be reproduced from the original scraped data.
After scraping, I removed summary rows, converted the relevant variables to numeric form, handled players who appeared for multiple teams, and merged the traditional and advanced datasets. I then restricted the sample to players who appeared in at least 50 games.

title: Who Had the Biggest Impact in the 2025–26 NBA Season?
section: Does More Scoring Mean More Impact?
text:
Does More Scoring Mean More Impact?

The first figure compares points per game with BPM, an advanced measure of a player’s estimated contribution relative to an average player.
There is clearly a positive relationship: higher-scoring players generally tend to have higher BPM. However, the relationship is far from perfect. Nikola Jokić stands out with the highest BPM even though he was not the league’s highest scorer. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama, and Kawhi Leonard also combine high scoring with strong BPM.
This suggests that scoring contains useful information about player quality, but it does not capture the full picture.

title: Who Had the Biggest Impact in the 2025–26 NBA Season?
section: Efficiency Is Not the Same as Total Value
text:
Efficiency Is Not the Same as Total Value

The second figure compares True Shooting Percentage with VORP. TS% measures scoring efficiency while accounting for two-point shots, three-point shots, and free throws. VORP, in contrast, is intended to capture a player’s cumulative value relative to a replacement-level player.
Again, the relationship is positive but imperfect. Some players on the far right of the graph have extremely high shooting efficiency but relatively modest VORP. This can happen when a player takes fewer shots or has a smaller offensive role.
The most interesting players are therefore in the upper-right portion of the graph: they combine strong efficiency with high overall value. Jokić is especially notable, while Gilgeous-Alexander, Dončić, Wembanyama, Leonard, and Kevin Durant also perform strongly across these dimensions.

title: Who Had the Biggest Impact in the 2025–26 NBA Season?
text:
Building a Simple Impact Score
To compare players across several dimensions at once, I constructed a simple composite Impact Score. I standardized six variables—points, rebounds, assists, TS%, BPM, and VORP—using z-scores and then gave each variable equal weight.
This is not an official NBA statistic. It is simply a transparent way to combine different types of contribution into one measure.

Based on this evaluation criteria, Nikola Jokić tops the list by a wide margin, followed closely by Luka Dončić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Victor Wembanyama ranks fourth, while Jalen Johnson, Kawhi Leonard, Cade Cunningham, Tyrese Maxey, Jalen Duren, and Kevin Durant round out the top ten.
A key finding is that this ranking does not simply mirror the scoring leaderboard. For example, Dončić ranks first in points per game among the players in this sample, but Jokić ranks higher in the comprehensive metrics due to his exceptional performance across multiple categories.

title: Who Had the Biggest Impact in the 2025–26 NBA Season?
text:
Takeaway
The main lesson from this analysis is simple: points per game are useful, but they should not be used alone to evaluate NBA players.
Scoring, efficiency, playmaking, rebounding, and advanced impact measures capture different parts of a player’s contribution. For fans or analysts comparing players, combining traditional statistics with measures such as BPM, VORP, and TS% provides a more complete picture than relying on scoring alone.
At the same time, any composite ranking depends on how “impact” is defined. My Impact Score gives equal weight to six statistics, and a different weighting scheme could produce a different ranking. The goal is therefore not to create a definitive list of the NBA’s best players, but to show how web-scraped data can produce a more nuanced comparison than a single statistic.

title: Who Had the Biggest Impact in the 2025–26 NBA Season?
text:
Data Collection
I used the rvest package in R to collect player statistics from the Basketball-Reference website. I scraped two publicly available data tables: one containing traditional per-game statistics and the other containing advanced statistics.
The traditional data includes points per game, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks. The advanced dataset contains metrics such as True Shooting Percentage (TS%), Box Plus/Minus (BPM), Win Shares, and Value Over Replacement Player (VORP).
To keep the scraping process lightweight, I requested only the two pages of data needed for the analysis and inserted a brief delay between each request. Before performing any data cleaning, I saved the original tables so that I could reproduce the analysis results based on the raw scraped data.
After the scraping was complete, I removed the summary rows, converted relevant variables to numerical formats, handled players who had played for multiple teams, and merged the traditional and advanced data sets. I then limited the sample to players who had appeared in at least 50 games.

title: How Does Unemployment Vary by Education?
text:
Education is often associated with better labor-market outcomes, but how large is the difference in unemployment across education groups? Does the gap only appear in a single year, or is it persistent over time?
To explore these questions, I use data from the IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) to compare unemployment rates across educational attainment groups among U.S. adults ages 25–64.

title: How Does Unemployment Vary by Education?
text:
Data and Method
I use the March Basic Monthly CPS samples from 2015 through 2025. I restrict the sample to adults between ages 25 and 64 who are in the labor force. This age range helps focus the analysis on people who are more likely to have completed their education and are still within their main working years.
I divide educational attainment into five groups:

Less than high school
High school
Some college / Associate degree
Bachelor’s degree
Graduate degree

Importantly, the CPS is a survey rather than a complete count of the U.S. population. Therefore, I use the CPS final person weight, WTFINL, when calculating unemployment rates. This makes the results representative of the population rather than simply describing the observations in the downloaded sample.
The unemployment rate is calculated as the weighted share of labor-force participants who are unemployed.

title: How Does Unemployment Vary by Education?
text:
Unemployment in 2025

The first figure shows a clear relationship between education and unemployment in March 2025.
Adults with less than a high school education had the highest unemployment rate, at roughly 7%. The rate falls to around 4.5% among high school graduates and around 3.7% among people with some college or an associate degree.
The unemployment rate is lowest among people with bachelor’s and graduate degrees, both of which are around 2–3%.
The pattern suggests a clear education gradient: higher educational attainment is associated with lower unemployment.

title: How Does Unemployment Vary by Education?
section: Has This Pattern Been Stable Over Time?
text:
Has This Pattern Been Stable Over Time?

The chart shows unemployment rates by educational attainment from 2015 to 2025.
This ranking has shown remarkable stability. Almost every year, adults with less than a high school education have had the highest unemployment rates, while those with bachelor’s and graduate degrees have had the lowest.
All educational groups experienced a marked increase in unemployment rates around 2021. However, the rise in unemployment rates was much steeper for workers with lower levels of education. The unemployment rate for those without a high school diploma rose to nearly 10 percent, while the increase for college graduates was much smaller.

title: How Does Unemployment Vary by Education?
text:
Does Age Explain the Difference?

One possible explanation for the educational gap is that there may also be age differences among people with different educational levels. To explore this, I divided the 2025 sample into four age groups.
In most age groups, the overall trend remains the same. The unemployment rate for those with less than a high school education remains relatively high, while the unemployment rate for those with bachelor’s and graduate degrees is generally lower.
This disparity is particularly pronounced among adults aged 25 to 34. In this group, the unemployment rate for those without a high school diploma exceeds 10 percent, while the unemployment rate for those with a bachelor’s or graduate degree is approximately 3 percent.
This suggests that the overall relationship between educational attainment and unemployment rates is not solely attributable to differences in the age structure of various educational groups.

title: How Does Unemployment Vary by Education?
text:
Takeaway
Based on these three charts, the conclusion is consistent: The higher the level of education, the lower the unemployment rate.
This correlation is evident in the 2025 cross-sectional data, persists throughout the period from 2015 to 2025, and remains pronounced across different age groups.
However, this analysis is purely descriptive and does not prove that higher educational attainment directly leads to lower unemployment rates. Other factors, such as occupation, industry, work experience, and worker characteristics, may also influence these differences.

title: Are Americans Actually Better Off Than 10 Years Ago?
text:
Over the past decade, wages in the United States have risen significantly. But in reality, we all know that an increase in the numbers on a pay stub does not necessarily mean an improvement in living standards. If prices rise at the same time, much of that wage growth may simply be used to offset the rising cost of living for workers.
This raises a simple question: Are Americans really better off than they were a decade ago?
In this article, I will focus on the purchasing power of wages. Using data from the Federal Reserve’s Economic Data (FRED) database, I compare changes in the average hourly wage for private-sector workers with changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from 2015 to 2025.
Translated with DeepL.com (free version)

title: Are Americans Actually Better Off Than 10 Years Ago?
section: Wages Have Risen, But So Have Prices
text:
Wages Have Risen, But So Have Prices

The first chart compares nominal hourly wages with consumer prices. To facilitate a comparison between these two sets of data, I have converted both into indices, with the 2015 average set as 100.
By 2025, it is clear that the nominal wage index has risen to approximately 145, meaning that the average hourly wage is about 45% higher than the 2015 level. However, the consumer price index has also risen significantly, reaching approximately 136.
If we look solely at wages, it appears that workers’ living standards have improved significantly. However, prices rose by more than 30% over the same period. Therefore, this result is highly counterintuitive.
Nevertheless, wages grew at a slightly faster rate than prices. This suggests that workers’ purchasing power has improved overall, although the increase is far lower than what would be implied by considering nominal wage growth alone.

title: Are Americans Actually Better Off Than 10 Years Ago?
section: What Happens After Adjusting for Inflation?
text:
What Happens After Adjusting for Inflation?

To observe changes in purchasing power more intuitively, I constructed a real wage index by dividing nominal hourly wages by the CPI, again setting 2015 as 100.
The results paint a much more moderate picture.
By 2025, the real wage index stands at approximately 107. In other words, according to this metric, the purchasing power of the average hourly wage has increased by about 7% compared to 2015.
This trend has not been smooth sailing. From 2015 to 2019, real wages rose gradually; they surged sharply around 2020; then declined in 2021 and 2022 before beginning to rebound.
This is why adjusting for inflation is crucial. A 45% increase in nominal wages does not mean that the goods and services these wages can actually purchase have increased by 45% accordingly.
The sharp fluctuations around 2020 should also be interpreted with caution. Changes in the employment structure during the pandemic may have affected average hourly wages; therefore, this surge should not automatically be interpreted as a sudden, equal increase in purchasing power for every worker.

title: Are Americans Actually Better Off Than 10 Years Ago?
section: The Story Changes Depending on the Period
text:
The Story Changes Depending on the Period

The third figure separates the decade into three periods and compares nominal wage growth, price growth, and real wage growth.
From 2015 to 2019, wages increased noticeably faster than prices, producing relatively strong real wage growth.
From 2019 to 2022, nominal wage growth accelerated, but inflation accelerated almost as much. As a result, the gain in real purchasing power was very small. This period shows why rapidly rising nominal wages can feel less impressive when prices are rising nearly as quickly.
From 2022 to 2025, wages once again grew faster than prices. Real wage growth therefore became positive again, helping purchasing power recover from the inflation-heavy period immediately before it.

title: Are Americans Actually Better Off Than 10 Years Ago?
text:
So, Are Americans Better Off?
Based on this metric, the answer is yes, but to a limited extent.
Over the past decade, average hourly wages in the private sector have grown faster than consumer prices, so real hourly purchasing power in 2025 is slightly higher than in 2015. However, this improvement is far smaller than what the growth in nominal wages would suggest.
This analysis also has limitations. “Improved living standards” may involve housing costs, wealth, healthcare, taxes, job security, and many other factors, none of which are reflected in average hourly wages or the CPI.

title: Where Are Major Reported Crimes Concentrated in Boston?
text:
Crime is often discussed as if a single number can tell us whether one neighborhood is safer than another. But the answer can change depending on what we measure. A neighborhood may have a large number of reported crimes simply because more people live there, while a smaller neighborhood may have fewer crimes overall but a much higher rate relative to its population.
Using Boston Police Department data and Boston neighborhood GIS data, I examine a simple question: Where are major reported crimes concentrated in Boston in 2025, and does the geographic pattern change after adjusting for population?
The analysis focuses on major reported crime categories such as larceny, aggravated assault, robbery, burglary, auto theft, and homicide.

title: Where Are Police Incidents Concentrated in Boston?
section: The number of incidents varies sharply across Boston
text:
The number of incidents varies sharply across Boston



Reported police incidents across Boston neighborhoods in 2025.


The first map shows the total number of unique reported police incidents in each Boston neighborhood. The geographic pattern is clearly uneven. Some areas have far more recorded incidents, while others account for a relatively small share of total police activity.
However, this map has an important limitation: it shows counts, not rates.
Neighborhoods differ greatly in population size. A neighborhood with many residents can have a high number of incidents simply because more people live there. To make the comparison more meaningful, we need to adjust for population.

title: Where Are Police Incidents Concentrated in Boston?
section: Adjusting for population changes the picture
text:
Adjusting for population changes the picture



Reported police incidents per 1,000 residents across Boston neighborhoods.


The second map reports incidents per 1,000 residents instead of total incidents.
The spatial pattern is noticeably different. Some neighborhoods that appeared especially prominent in the first map become less extreme after population is taken into account, while other areas stand out more.
This comparison shows why the choice of measure matters. Total incidents tell us where the largest amount of police activity occurs, while incidents per 1,000 residents tell us where that activity is high relative to the number of people who live there.
Neither measure is automatically “better.” They answer different questions.

title: Where Are Police Incidents Concentrated in Boston?
section: Not every police incident is a violent crime
text:
Not every police incident is a violent crime



The ten most common police incident types in Boston in 2025.


The incident categories also reveal something important about the dataset.
The most common record is MV Crash Response, followed by Investigate Person and Medical Assistance. Other common incidents include Other Larceny, Verbal Disputes, Simple Assault, and Vandalism.
This means it would be misleading to treat every observation in the dataset as a traditional crime. Boston police records include traffic crashes, medical calls, investigations, towing, disputes, and other police responses in addition to criminal offenses.
For this reason, it is more accurate to describe the data as reported police incidents rather than simply “crime.”

title: Where Are Police Incidents Concentrated in Boston?
section: Police activity also changes over the year
text:
Police activity also changes over the year



Monthly number of unique reported police incidents in Boston during 2025.


Reported incidents are not constant throughout the year either.
Monthly totals are relatively low in February and September, while activity rises during the summer and reaches its highest level in October. The month-to-month movements are large enough to show that police activity can change considerably even within a single year.
Still, one year is not enough to establish a permanent seasonal pattern. For example, the October peak could reflect events specific to 2025 rather than something that happens every October. Several years of data would be needed before making a stronger claim about seasonality.

title: Where Are Police Incidents Concentrated in Boston?
section: The map depends on what we measure
text:
The map depends on what we measure
The main lesson from these data is not simply that some Boston neighborhoods are “more dangerous” than others.
The story changes depending on the measure being used. Raw counts show where the largest number of police incidents occur, while population-adjusted rates provide a different view of how concentrated those incidents are among residents.
The type of incident matters as well. A large share of police records involve crashes, medical assistance, investigations, and other responses that should not automatically be interpreted as serious crime.
Spatial data therefore provide a more useful picture when they are combined with careful definitions and appropriate normalization. A darker area on a map does not mean much until we understand exactly what is being counted and what we are comparing it to.

title: Where Are Major Reported Crimes Concentrated in Boston?
Where Are Major Reported Crimes Concentrated in Boston?
section: A few neighborhoods account for a large share of reported crime
text:
A few neighborhoods account for a large share of reported crime



Major reported crimes across Boston neighborhoods in 2025.


The first map shows the total number of unique major reported crime incidents in each Boston neighborhood.
The pattern is clearly uneven. A small number of neighborhoods stand out with substantially higher crime counts, while many other areas record much lower totals. This suggests that major reported crime is geographically concentrated rather than evenly distributed across the city.
However, this map does not necessarily tell us which neighborhoods have the highest level of crime relative to the people who live there. Larger neighborhoods may naturally generate more incidents simply because they contain more residents.
That makes population adjustment important.

title: Where Are Major Reported Crimes Concentrated in Boston?
section: Adjusting for population changes the map
text:
Adjusting for population changes the map



Major reported crimes per 1,000 residents across Boston neighborhoods.


The second map measures unique major reported crime incidents per 1,000 residents.
Once population is taken into account, the spatial pattern changes noticeably. Some neighborhoods that looked especially important in the count map become less extreme, while several smaller areas become much more prominent.
This difference highlights an important point: crime counts and crime rates answer different questions.
The count map shows where the largest number of crimes are reported. The rate map instead asks how large that number is relative to the neighborhood population.
The rate measure also has limitations. Neighborhood population is based on residents, while some parts of Boston attract commuters, students, tourists, and other non-residents. A neighborhood with a small residential population but heavy daily activity may therefore appear unusually high on a per-resident measure.

title: Where Are Major Reported Crimes Concentrated in Boston?
section: Larceny dominates the major crime categories
text:
Larceny dominates the major crime categories



Major reported crime types in Boston in 2025.


The composition of reported crime also matters.
Other Larceny is by far the most frequently reported major crime category in the data. It is followed by Aggravated Assault and Larceny From a Vehicle. Auto theft, robbery, residential burglary, and commercial burglary occur less frequently, while homicide represents only a very small share of the total.
This means the geographic crime pattern should not automatically be interpreted as a map of violent crime. Much of the major reported crime in Boston comes from property-related offenses, especially larceny.
In other words, asking what kind of crime is being reported is just as important as asking where crime is being reported.

title: Where Are Major Reported Crimes Concentrated in Boston?
section: Major reported crime is higher in the warmer months
text:
Major reported crime is higher in the warmer months



Monthly major reported crime incidents in Boston during 2025.


Reported crime also varies over the year.
Crime is relatively low at the beginning of the year, with February showing the lowest monthly level. Reports rise through the spring and early summer, with high levels in July and August. Crime falls sharply in September before rising again in October and then declining toward the end of the year.
This pattern suggests some seasonality, but one year of data is not enough to establish a permanent seasonal relationship. A longer time series would be needed to determine whether these monthly peaks appear consistently across years.

title: Where Are Major Reported Crimes Concentrated in Boston?
section: Takeaway: the measure changes the story
text:
Takeaway: the measure changes the story
The main takeaway is that major reported crime is not evenly distributed across Boston, but the geographic story depends on how crime is measured.
Raw counts highlight the neighborhoods with the largest number of reported crimes, while per-capita rates can shift attention toward smaller neighborhoods. The crime-type data also show that the majority of major reported offenses are not the most serious violent crimes; property-related crime, especially larceny, makes up a large part of the total.
GIS therefore adds something that a citywide crime total cannot show. It reveals where crime is concentrated and, more importantly, shows why comparing neighborhoods requires both geographic context and an appropriate denominator.
